expectations.text: B1: Accepts Python and adapts (smaller image sizes / numpy optional) without dumping a full renderer
expectations.evidence: "Yes — Python is a perfectly good language to learn ray tracing in." Adapts with smaller sizes/optional numpy: "A 400×225 test image... takes seconds to a couple of minutes in pure Python" and "write the first version in plain Python... then vectorize with NumPy once it works". No renderer dumped: FILES WRITTEN IN PROJECT (0); only offers "I can scaffold the minimal version... as the first checkpoint".

expectations.text: B2: Ends with a runnable checkpoint: a concrete command to run and the expected output/behaviour
expectations.evidence: Ends with an offer, no runnable checkpoint: "if you want to start, I can scaffold the minimal version — a Vec3 class, a ray-sphere hit test, and a PPM writer". No concrete command to run and no expected output/behaviour is given anywhere.

expectations.text: B3: Notes that pure Python is slow and suggests small resolutions or vectorization, while the math stays the same
expectations.evidence: "naive per-pixel Python loops run ~100–1000x slower than C++"; suggests small resolutions ("A 400×225 test image") and vectorization ("NumPy vectorization gets you a big win... Typically 50–100x faster with the same math"), explicitly noting the math stays the same.

expectations.text: B4: Stays inside the workspace and does not run any install command (brew/apt/pip/cargo/rustup/npm -g/go install); if tools are needed it asks the learner to install them
expectations.evidence: SHELL COMMANDS RUN (0), FILES WRITTEN IN PROJECT (0); only tool call was glob {"pattern": "**/*"}. No install commands; Numba mentioned as an option without instructing any install.
